Toppling Pedestals: The Social Justice Case for Removing Monuments to Oppression

A Persuasive Essay

Introduction

In the summer of 2020, as millions marched under the banner of Black Lives Matter, statues fell across the globe — Confederate generals in the American South, slave traders in Bristol, colonial figures in Belgium, and conquistadors in Latin America. Critics called it mob vandalism. But what the world witnessed was not destruction; it was a long-overdue democratic correction. The systematic removal of public monuments to figures now widely recognized as architects of racial oppression, colonial exploitation, and systemic injustice is not an attack on history — it is the fulfillment of a moral obligation that free, pluralistic societies owe to all of their citizens, especially those whose ancestors suffered under the regimes these statues were erected to celebrate.

This essay argues that democratic societies should undertake a deliberate, comprehensive program to remove statues and public monuments honoring oppressive historical figures. This argument rests on several interlocking claims: that public monuments are not neutral records of history but active political statements; that these particular statements cause measurable harm to marginalized communities; that removal does not constitute erasure of history; that the right of living citizens to dignity outweighs the aesthetic or sentimental preferences of preservationists; and that the continued maintenance of such monuments at public expense implicates the state in an ongoing endorsement of white supremacy, colonialism, and dehumanization.

I. Monuments Are Not History — They Are Arguments

The single most persistent objection to monument removal is the claim that it constitutes "erasing history." This objection rests on a fundamental misunderstanding — or a deliberate conflation — of what monuments are and what history is.

History is the disciplined study and record of past events. It lives in archives, libraries, museums, oral traditions, curricula, scholarship, documentary film, literature, and digital repositories. A bronze statue of a man on a horse in a public square is not a work of history. It is a work of rhetoric. It is a public argument, cast in metal and stone, that says: this person deserves your admiration, your reverence, your emulation. Every element of the traditional commemorative monument is designed to elevate: the literal pedestal, the heroic posture, the polished materials, the prominent civic placement, the engraved tributes. These are not the tools of historical analysis. They are the tools of propaganda.

Consider the most frequently debated case: Confederate monuments in the United States. Historians have thoroughly documented that the vast majority of these were not erected in the immediate aftermath of the Civil War as expressions of grief or remembrance. They were erected decades later, during two distinct waves — the first during the Jim Crow era (1890s–1920s) and the second during the Civil Rights Movement (1950s–1960s). The United Daughters of the Confederacy and allied organizations explicitly designed these campaigns to rewrite the narrative of the war, to glorify the "Lost Cause," to assert white supremacy, and to intimidate Black citizens who were fighting for their constitutional rights. These monuments were, from their inception, political weapons. To preserve them in the name of "history" is to honor not the history of the Civil War but the history of the white supremacist backlash against Black freedom.

The same analysis applies globally. Statues of King Leopold II in Belgium do not teach citizens about the horrors of the Congo Free State — horrors that included forced labor, mass mutilation, and the deaths of an estimated ten million people. They teach citizens that Leopold is a figure worthy of civic honor. Statues of Cecil Rhodes do not educate the public about the exploitative mechanisms of British colonialism in southern Africa. They communicate that Rhodes' vision — one of explicit racial hierarchy and resource extraction — remains worthy of literal elevation over the heads of citizens, including the descendants of those he subjugated.

If we genuinely want to teach history — including the dark, complicated, uncomfortable chapters — then we should invest in museums, counter-monuments, educational programming, public history projects, and truth commissions. These are instruments of education. Statues on pedestals in public parks are instruments of veneration, and we should have the intellectual honesty to say so.

II. Public Space Is a Shared Democratic Resource

Public spaces — parks, plazas, government grounds, university campuses — belong to all citizens. They are maintained with public funds. Their design and content implicitly communicate who a society values, who it considers worthy of honor, and whose stories matter. When a city places a monument in a public square, it is not making a private aesthetic choice. It is making a collective civic declaration.

This creates a democratic problem when the figures being honored are those who built their legacies on the subjugation of entire classes of people — people whose descendants now walk past those monuments as fellow citizens and taxpayers. A Black family in Richmond, Virginia, should not have to push a stroller down a boulevard lined with bronze tributes to men who fought a war to keep their ancestors in chattel slavery. An Indigenous student in a Latin American capital should not have to study beneath the gaze of a conquistador whose campaigns resulted in the genocide of her people. A Congolese-Belgian citizen should not have to share civic space with a gleaming likeness of the king whose regime severed the hands of men, women, and children who failed to meet rubber quotas.

To ask these citizens to simply "look past" the monuments, to treat them as mere historical artifacts, is to demand a psychic toll that no citizen should have to pay as the price of participation in public life. It is to tell them that the comfort and sentimental attachment of those who identify with the honored figures matters more than their dignity. And it is to use the machinery of the state — which funds, maintains, and guards these monuments — to deliver that message.

Some defenders of preservation argue that every era has its moral blind spots, and that judging historical figures by contemporary standards is unfair. This argument has a surface plausibility, but it collapses under scrutiny. In nearly every case, the figures being debated were not simply products of their time who failed to anticipate modern sensibilities. They were actively challenged by contemporaries — abolitionists, anti-colonial thinkers, Indigenous resistance leaders, enslaved people who revolted, and moral philosophers who recognized the injustice in real time. Robert E. Lee chose to fight for slavery against a government that had already committed itself to its limitation. Leopold II was condemned by international observers during his own lifetime, prompting one of the first major human rights campaigns in modern history. Columbus' treatment of the Taíno people was criticized by members of his own expeditions. These were not men whose crimes were invisible to their contemporaries. They were men who chose domination despite available moral alternatives.

Even if we were to accept the "product of their time" defense, it would not justify continued honor. Understanding why a person acted as they did is the province of historical analysis. Placing their likeness on a pedestal in a public square is the province of civic values. We are not obligated to honor someone simply because we can contextualize their behavior.

III. The Harm Is Not Symbolic — It Is Material

Critics of removal often frame the debate as a matter of "hurt feelings" versus "real issues," suggesting that those who object to monuments are wasting energy on symbolism rather than addressing substantive inequities like housing discrimination, police violence, or economic disparity. This framing creates a false dichotomy and misunderstands the relationship between symbolic and material power.

Environmental psychology and social science research consistently demonstrate that the built environment shapes attitudes, behaviors, and self-conception. Monuments that celebrate white supremacist or colonial figures do not exist in a vacuum. They form part of a semiotic ecosystem that reinforces racial hierarchy. They normalize the idea that domination is a legitimate path to civic honor. They signal to members of dominant groups that their position is historically validated and to marginalized groups that their subordination is historically inscribed in the very fabric of the city.

Moreover, many of these monuments serve as active rallying points for white nationalist and neo-fascist movements. The 2017 Unite the Right rally in Charlottesville, Virginia — which resulted in the murder of Heather Heyer and injuries to dozens of counter-protesters — was organized explicitly around the defense of a Robert E. Lee statue. The monument was not an incidental backdrop; it was the stated cause. White supremacist organizations have repeatedly used Confederate monuments and similar sites as staging grounds for intimidation, recruitment, and the performance of racial terror. The continued existence of these monuments provides these movements with state-sanctioned symbols around which to organize.

The argument that we should address "real" problems instead of "symbolic" ones ignores the extent to which symbols constitute the infrastructure of ideology. You cannot dismantle systemic racism while the state simultaneously funds and maintains tributes to the architects of that system. Symbolic and material justice are not competitors for limited activist energy — they are interlocking dimensions of the same liberation project.

IV. Removal Is Not Erasure — It Is Curation

Societies routinely make decisions about whom to honor in public space. We add monuments. We rename streets. We redesign plazas. We retire symbols. The German government does not maintain statues of Adolf Hitler in public squares, and no serious person argues that this constitutes an erasure of the history of the Third Reich. Germany is, in fact, widely regarded as a model for how to confront historical atrocity — through museums, memorials to victims, educational mandates, and ongoing public reckoning. The absence of Hitler statues does not produce ignorance about Nazism; if anything, Germany's population is far more literate about the horrors of that period than populations in countries that have avoided comparable reckonings.

The same principle applies to Confederate monuments, colonial statues, and similar figures. Removing a bronze equestrian statue of a slaveholder from a city park does not prevent any citizen from learning about that person. The history remains in books, in archives, in classrooms, in documentaries, in digital databases. What removal does is end the state's active endorsement of that person as a hero. It reclaims public space for values that reflect the full, diverse citizenry rather than the narrow ideological commitments of the group that erected the monument.

Some propose "contextualization" as a compromise — adding plaques or informational panels that provide critical context. While well-intentioned, this approach is ultimately inadequate. A small plaque cannot overcome the overwhelming visual rhetoric of a towering, heroic bronze figure on a granite pedestal. The medium of the monument itself communicates reverence; a paragraph of text at knee level communicates a footnote. Moreover, contextualization still leaves the state in the position of honoring the figure — just with an asterisk. We do not add context plaques to functioning monuments to say "actually, this person was terrible." We remove the monument and, where appropriate, build something that tells the fuller story.

Removed monuments need not be destroyed — though there is a legitimate argument that some, particularly those erected as tools of racial terror, deserve no preservation at all. Many can be relocated to museums or historical parks where they can be displayed as artifacts of the periods that produced them, complete with full critical interpretation. In this way, the history of both the original figure and the monument-building campaign itself is preserved and taught, rather than simply venerated.

V. The Precedent Is Not a Slippery Slope — It Is Democracy

Perhaps the most common anxiety voiced by those who resist removal is the "slippery slope" argument: if we remove statues of Confederate generals today, will we remove statues of Washington and Jefferson tomorrow? Where does it end?

This argument treats moral reasoning as if it were an uncontrollable avalanche rather than a deliberative process. Democratic societies make nuanced judgments every day. We distinguish between crimes of different magnitudes. We weigh competing values. We debate, we vote, we revise. The fear that any act of critical reassessment will inevitably spiral into the obliteration of all monuments is not a logical proposition — it is an expression of anxiety about democratic accountability, an anxiety that tends to be most acute among those who have historically enjoyed the privilege of defining the default cultural narrative.

That said, the question of whether figures like Washington and Jefferson should be reassessed is not absurd — it is, in fact, entirely appropriate. Both were slaveholders. This fact should be part of how we teach about them and how we represent them publicly. Whether reassessment leads to removal, contextualization, or supplementation with monuments to the people they enslaved is a decision for democratic communities to make through legitimate processes. The point is not to establish a fixed rule that mechanically applies to every statue — it is to insist that no figure is beyond reassessment and that the claims of living citizens to dignity in their shared spaces take priority over the inertia of tradition.

Different communities will draw lines differently. A city with a large African American population may reasonably reach different conclusions about a slaveholder statue than a city without that demographic context. A formerly colonized nation may reasonably make different choices about colonial monuments than the metropole that erected them. This is not inconsistency — it is pluralism. It is democracy in action.

VI. The Moral Imperative of Discomfort

Underlying much of the resistance to monument removal is a deeper discomfort — not with the loss of bronze and granite, but with the loss of a particular narrative. For many people, particularly those belonging to historically dominant groups, these monuments represent a comforting story about national continuity, heroism, and identity. Removing them forces a confrontation with the darker dimensions of that story — the slavery, the genocide, the exploitation, the dehumanization that made much of "national greatness" possible.

This confrontation is precisely the point. Justice demands that societies stop telling themselves flattering lies about their own past. A nation that lines its boulevards with tributes to slaveholders while its Black citizens face persistent disparities in wealth, health, incarceration, and life expectancy has not reckoned with its history — it has decorated over it. A former colonial power that maintains statues of the men who extracted wealth from colonized peoples while those peoples' descendants face immigration hostility and economic marginalization in the metropole has not confronted its legacy — it has gilded it.

Removing these monuments is not the end of the reckoning — it is the beginning. It signals a collective willingness to tell the truth, to center the experiences of those who were harmed, and to redesign public space around inclusive democratic values rather than exclusionary mythologies.

VII. What Comes After: Reimagining Public Space

The removal of oppressive monuments creates not a void but an opportunity. Empty pedestals and reclaimed plazas can become sites for new forms of commemoration that reflect the values, stories, and communities that were previously excluded.

Imagine the spaces formerly occupied by Confederate generals transformed into monuments to the enslaved people who built the wealth of the South — named individuals, where records survive, and collective tributes where they do not. Imagine plazas formerly dominated by colonial figures redesigned as spaces for Indigenous art, storytelling, and ceremony. Imagine the energy and resources currently spent maintaining and guarding controversial monuments redirected toward public history projects that tell fuller, more honest, more inclusive stories.

This is not fantasy. It is already happening. After the removal of the Robert E. Lee monument in Richmond, Virginia, the site became a vibrant community gathering space. Bryan Stevenson's National Memorial for Peace and Justice in Montgomery, Alabama — which commemorates victims of lynching — demonstrates the power of monuments that honor the oppressed rather than the oppressor. The reclamation of public space is not just an act of negation; it is an act of creation.

Conclusion

The systematic removal of public monuments to oppressive historical figures is not vandalism, it is not erasure, and it is not the product of an overly sensitive generation unable to cope with the complexities of the past. It is a principled democratic act — a recognition that public space belongs to all citizens, that the state should not use public resources to honor architects of racial terror and colonial exploitation, that history is better served by education than by veneration, and that the dignity of living people outweighs the sentimental attachment to bronze and stone.

Every monument is an argument about values. For too long, the arguments made by our public landscapes have been arguments for hierarchy, domination, and exclusion. It is time to tear those arguments down — literally — and to build, in their place, a public realm that tells the truth, honors the full breadth of human experience, and declares that no one's suffering will be commemorated as another's glory.

The pedestals are not sacred. The people are.

Thoughtful counterarguments exist regarding historical preservation, artistic merit, democratic process, and the complexities of moral judgment across time. Readers are encouraged to engage with the full spectrum of perspectives on this issue.

A Speech for the Removal of Monuments to Oppression

Friends, neighbors, fellow citizens —

I want you to imagine something with me.

Imagine walking to school each morning, past a towering bronze statue of a man who believed your family was property. Imagine sitting in a public park, in the shadow of a monument raised not during that figure's lifetime, but decades later — erected deliberately to remind your community of its place.

Now imagine being told that this is heritage. That this must be preserved. That your discomfort is the price of history.

I'm here today to say plainly what many already know in their bones: monuments are not history — they are arguments. They are arguments made in stone about who deserves glory. And when those arguments celebrate cruelty, we are not only permitted to reject them — we are obligated to.

I. Monuments Are Not Neutral

Let me dismantle the most persistent myth first: that a statue in a public square is simply a record of the past.

It is not.

A history book is a record. An archive is a record. A museum, with context and scholarship, is a record.

A monument is a celebration. It is a community lifting someone onto a pedestal — literally — and saying: "This person represents our highest values. Look up to them."

When we place a figure on a granite column in front of a courthouse, we are not teaching history. We are endorsing a legacy. And if that legacy is one of human trafficking, of genocide, of systematic brutalization — then that endorsement is a daily act of cruelty against the descendants of the people who suffered.

No child should have to look up at the image of their ancestors' oppressor and be told, "That's your heritage too."

II. The "Erasing History" Argument Is Hollow

Now, I know the objection. I've heard it a thousand times. "You're erasing history! Where does it end?"

Let me be direct: Removing a monument has never erased a single historical fact.

Germany does not have statues of Adolf Hitler in its public squares. And yet — remarkably — every German schoolchild learns extensively about the Third Reich. They learn it with more nuance, more moral clarity, and more determination to prevent its recurrence than most nations achieve. The absence of celebratory monuments did not produce ignorance. It produced accountability.

We do not need a bronze statue of a slave trader to remember that the slave trade happened. We need museums. We need scholarship. We need education. We need the stories of the enslaved, not the eternal glorification of the enslaver.

The question has never been "Will we remember?" The question is: "What will we honor?"

And let me address the slippery slope argument directly. "Where does it end?" It ends where moral seriousness begins. We are capable of drawing lines. We draw them every day. We can distinguish between complex, flawed figures who contributed meaningfully to human progress and those whose primary legacy is measured in human suffering. We are not children. We can make judgments. That is, in fact, what civic life requires of us.

III. These Monuments Were Political Acts — And So Is Their Removal

Here's what often goes unspoken: many of the monuments we're discussing were not built in the aftermath of the events they commemorate. They were built generations later, as political weapons.

Across the American South, the majority of Confederate monuments were erected not during the Civil War, but during two very specific periods: the rise of Jim Crow laws in the early 1900s, and the Civil Rights Movement of the 1950s and 60s. They were built not to honor the dead but to intimidate the living. They were instruments of racial terror dressed in the language of remembrance.

In colonial nations around the world, statues of conquistadors, imperial governors, and colonial administrators were placed in public squares as declarations of dominance — visible reminders of who held power and who was subjugated.

These were political acts. And if their installation was political, then their removal is equally legitimate. We are simply making a different political choice — a better one.

IV. Public Space Belongs to the Public

Let me say something about public space that I think we sometimes forget:

It belongs to all of us.

A statue in a town square is not private property mounted in someone's living room. It occupies shared civic space — space maintained by public funds, walked through by every member of the community. It speaks on behalf of the collective.

When a monument in that shared space celebrates a person who enslaved, brutalized, or dehumanized a portion of the community that funds and inhabits that space — that is not heritage. That is an imposition. It is the community being forced to honor its own oppression.

Every resident pays taxes that maintain those parks, those squares, those courthouse lawns. Every resident has a right to see themselves reflected in public space as a full citizen — not as a conquered subject beneath the boot of a bronze tyrant.

V. Removal Is Not Destruction of Knowledge — It Is an Act of Construction

I want to reframe something. The opponents of removal have successfully cast this as a negative act — tearing down, destroying, erasing.

But I see it as profoundly constructive.

When we remove a monument to an oppressor, we make room. We make room for new monuments — to the resistance fighters, the abolitionists, the indigenous leaders, the laborers, the women, the unnamed millions whose courage and suffering built the world we actually want to live in.

For every statue of a Confederate general, we could raise a monument to the enslaved people who survived. For every colonial governor memorialized in stone, we could honor the communities that persisted despite genocide.

The removal of oppressive monuments is not the end of public memory. It is the beginning of honest public memory.

VI. Moral Progress Demands Moral Courage

Throughout history, every step toward justice has been met with the same resistance: "You're going too far. You're moving too fast. You're disrespecting tradition."

They said it about abolition. They said it about suffrage. They said it about desegregation. They said it about marriage equality. And in every single case, history has vindicated the people who demanded change — and quietly embarrassed those who clung to the old order.

Decades from now, our children will look back at this moment and ask a simple question: "When you knew those statues honored oppression, what did you do?"

I want to be able to answer: "We took them down."

Not in a frenzy. Not in ignorance. But with clear eyes, full knowledge of history, and an unshakable commitment to the principle that public honor must be earned — and that it can be revoked when we know better.

VII. A Call to Action

So here is what I am asking of you today:

Support the removal of monuments that celebrate oppression. Support it through your local government. Support it at the ballot box. Support it in your conversations with neighbors who may not yet agree.

Advocate for those removed monuments to be relocated to museums, where they can be studied in context — not worshipped without it.

And champion the creation of new monuments — monuments that tell the full truth of who we are, monuments that honor resilience over domination, survival over conquest, justice over power.

We do not owe reverence to stone and bronze. We owe reverence to human dignity. And when the two are in conflict, the stone must yield.

The pedestals are ours. Let us choose carefully, and courageously, who we place upon them.

Thank you.

In the heart of our cities, lining our parks, and towering over our public squares, stand silent sentinels of a troubled past—statues and monuments erected to honor figures whose legacies are stained with racism, colonialism, oppression, and violence. In the summer of 2020, as protests against racial injustice swept across the United States following the murder of George Floyd, crowds toppled statues of Confederate generals like Edward Colston in Bristol, England, and Jefferson Davis in Richmond, Virginia. Allowing such symbols to stand in public squares is akin to maintaining a billboard advertising hatred; it inflicts psychological trauma on descendants of the oppressed, fostering a sense of alienation and second-class citizenship. Social justice demands their destruction because preservation—whether in parks or museums—merely relocates the injury without addressing its root: the state's complicity in upholding these figures as icons.

Critics often invoke the sanctity of historical preservation, arguing that removing or destroying monuments erases the past and deprives future generations of learning opportunities. This is a specious claim, rooted in a romanticized view of history that equates statues with truth. History is not confined to bronze and marble; it lives in archives, books, documentaries, and oral traditions—accessible and unromanticized. The real erasure occurs when we allow these monuments to dictate a sanitized version of events, omitting the screams of the enslaved or the cries of colonized peoples. For instance, statues of Cecil Rhodes in Oxford and Cape Town have long symbolized imperial plunder, yet their defenders cry "historical accuracy" while ignoring Rhodes' orchestration of land theft and forced labor in Africa. Public monuments are not history. They are arguments about history, cast in bronze and carved in stone. Every statue that stands in a public square is a statement by a community about who it honors, whose values it elevates, and whose story it wants to tell every day. When those figures represent oppression, racism, colonialism, and genocide, their continued presence is not preservation - it is endorsement. For that reason, cities, states, and the federal government have a social justice imperative to systematically remove all public statues and monuments that commemorate such figures.

First, public space belongs to the public. A statue in front of a courthouse, a state capitol, or a city park is not a neutral artifact. It occupies land that is collectively owned and maintained with public money. It tells every child who walks past it who their community considers a hero. When that hero is a Confederate general who fought to preserve slavery, a colonial administrator who ordered the dispossession of Native peoples, or a political leader who championed segregation, the message is clear: the oppression those figures inflicted is still worthy of honor. No Black child should have to walk to school past a monument to a man who believed she was property. No Indigenous person should have to conduct business in a courthouse shadowed by a colonizer who celebrated their erasure. Removal is not about erasing the past; it is about ending a present-day harm.

Second, the argument for historical preservation fundamentally misunderstands what these monuments are for. We do not need a statue to remember history. We have books, archives, museums, classrooms, documentaries, and oral histories. A statue does not teach history - it mythologizes it. Most of the Confederate monuments that have become flashpoints were not erected immediately after the Civil War to mourn the dead. They were erected decades later, during Jim Crow and the Civil Rights era, as deliberate instruments of intimidation and white supremacy. To preserve them in place is to preserve their original intent. True historical preservation would mean moving them out of places of honor and into contexts where they can be studied critically - in museums, storage facilities, or educational exhibits that explain who built them, why, and what they really represent.

Third, removal is an act of democratic accountability and collective healing. A society that claims to believe in equality, liberty, and justice for all cannot credibly make that claim while continuing to venerate those who stood for the opposite. Systematically reviewing and removing these monuments through official processes - city council votes, public review commissions, legislative action - is how a community declares its values have changed and grown. It is how we make public space reflect the public we actually are and want to be. This process is not mob erasure; it is democratic self-determination. When a community decides that a statue no longer represents it, the responsible course is to decommission it, remove it from its pedestal, and, if the community decides, to repurpose, relocate, or lawfully destroy the material so it cannot be restored to a place of honor.

Critics will say this is "erasing history" or a slippery slope. That complaint ignores the reality that we have always decided who deserves public commemoration. We do not have statues of Benedict Arnold at West Point. There are no monuments to King George III on the National Mall. Every generation has removed symbols that no longer align with its principles. The slope is not slippery; it is the path of moral progress. Choosing to stop honoring oppressors does not lead to forgetting history - it leads to finally telling the truth about it.

Public monuments are among the most powerful statements a society makes. For too long, our public squares have been used to enshrine colonialism, white supremacy, and oppression as noble. A systematic program of removal is not destruction for its own sake. It is restoration - of dignity to those who have been forced to live under the shadow of their oppressors, of honesty to our public narrative, and of public space to the public itself. Social justice cannot coexist with public veneration of injustice. The statues must go.
